concept.shortExplanation: Everything that decides whether training works sits outside the model: learning rate, batch size, initialisation, how long you run. Small batches give noisy gradients that sometimes help you escape bad regions and sometimes stop you settling anywhere. Large learning rates cover ground until they diverge. There is no setting that is correct in general, only settings that are correct for a budget — and you are about to spend one.
concept.ahaMoment: The loss curve tells you what happened, not why. Two runs with identical final loss can have taken completely different routes, and only one of them would have survived a slightly harder dataset.

levels.title: Read the Curve
levels.instructions: Four real training runs, four different learning rates. Match each loss curve to the rate that produced it. The runs are executed live before you answer.
hints: Each line really was trained at one of the four rates on offer — read the shape, not just where it ends. A rate that's too small barely moves the loss at all; one that's too large can spike before it (maybe) settles.

Read them as a spectrum: the flattest curve is the smallest rate, the one that plunges cleanly to the lowest loss is a well-tuned middle rate, and any curve that shoots up high before coming back down is the largest rate — it's covering too much ground per step to be stable.

Checked against this exact run (seed 13): the curve running 0.673 → 0.017 is lr = 1; the one barely moving, 0.713 → 0.703, is lr = 0.001; the one drifting down slowly, 0.708 → 0.559, is lr = 0.05; and the one spiking above 13 before settling near 4.9 is lr = 10 — it never recovers within these 120 epochs.

levels.title: Batch Size Trade-off
levels.instructions: Same network, fixed epoch count. Find the batch size that reaches the lowest validation loss, and notice what the gradient noise is doing at each end of the range.
hints: Epochs are fixed here, so batch size decides how many weight updates you actually get: a batch of 1 gets far more updates than a batch of 128 in the same 250 epochs. Try the small end of the range first.

Once you've picked a batch size, the learning rate needs raising to match — a small batch with the default learning rate is stable but slow, and small batch plus a low rate wastes most of those extra updates. Push both down in batch size and up in learning rate together.

Checked directly: batch size 1 at the default learning rate (0.08) already clears 1 star (loss ≈ 0.0026); raising the learning rate to 0.15 at batch size 1 clears 3 stars (loss ≈ 0.0017, target ≤ 0.002). At the other end, batch size 128 fails to pass even at the maximum allowed learning rate (0.5, loss ≈ 0.106) — too few, too noisy updates to recover in this budget.

levels.title: The Compute Budget
levels.instructions: You have a fixed budget of gradient updates. Spend it — choose architecture, learning rate, batch size and epochs — to reach the lowest validation loss. Every configuration is actually trained before it is scored.
hints: The budget is spent in updates, not epochs — a smaller batch size or more epochs both burn through it faster. Check the projected-updates meter before you run; overspending gets charged straight back into your score as a penalty on top of the loss.

Architecture size isn't what's holding this back on the spiral dataset — the activation is. tanh's derivative shrinks the gradient the same way it did in the vanishing-gradient chapter, and no amount of budget rescues it. A rectifying activation doesn't have that problem.

Checked directly: tanh scores 0 stars at every batch size and learning rate tried, spending the full 6000-update budget and still stuck around 0.55–0.65 loss. Swapping to ReLU with the same architecture, learning rate 0.2 and batch size 16 reaches about 0.086 loss — 3 stars — using exactly the 6000-update budget.
